cands.bio: Republican U.S. Representative for California's 40th District, in Congress since 2021 (first for the 39th District). Served in the California Assembly (District 65) 2014–2016. Former business owner and financial analyst, and 21 years as community liaison and Asian affairs director for Rep. Ed Royce.

controversies.text: Federal records show $24,710 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; $126,629 from individuals passed through that PAC in 2025-26; 2 trips paid for by the American Israel Education Foundation, AIPAC's affiliate; 3 staff trips paid for by that foundation.
Missed 5 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (0.7%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 2, 2025-03-31 to 2025-03-31.

In November 2018, as late-counted ballots erased Kim's early lead in the 39th District race, her campaign accused Gil Cisneros's campaign of harassing and intimidating vote counters. Cisneros's campaign called the claim false. Kim then conceded and called Cisneros to congratulate him.

endorsements.text: 2026: U.S. Rep. James Gallagher (R) and state Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones (R).
2026: Americans for Prosperity Action and the Orange County Register Editorial Board.

cands.gaps: We could not find the year Kim moved to California. We found no documented stance of hers on data centers or local development approvals. We found no record on her position on gun laws, school choice or teacher pay, limits on investor or foreign purchases of homes and land, or abortion beyond one statement tied to the Hyde Amendment. We found no stated pledge about refusing particular kinds of donations. She did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey in 2022, 2024 or 2026. The Ballotpedia page was cut off partway through its 118th Congress key votes, so nothing from that section was used. Kim's 2026 campaign-site text was read only as quoted on Ballotpedia and on the campaign's own homepage.

qual.background: Served in the California Assembly 2014–2016 and has been a U.S. Representative since 2021. Earlier she spent 21 years as a congressional staffer for Rep. Ed Royce, and she was a financial analyst and clothing-business owner.
qual.why: Prior state legislative office, about five years in Congress, and long senior congressional staff experience fit the lawmaking, oversight and constituent-service role.
qual.label: Prior state legislative office, about five years in Congress, and long senior congressional staff experience fit the lawmaking, oversight and constituent-service role.

back-police-order.evidence: Her 2026 campaign site says she has always supported law enforcement, opposes 'defund the police' policies and stands for law and order.

end-homestead-tax.evidence: Her 2016 Assembly reelection platform included opposing changes to Proposition 13, which limits property taxes.

stop-data-centers.evidence: Her 2026 campaign site says she supports the President's AI Action Plan, which it says 'expands access to American AI infrastructure.' It does not mention data centers by name.

pro-life.evidence: After voting against the Equality Act in 2021, she said the bill 'opens the door to ending the decades-long bipartisan Hyde Amendment' (the federal limit on abortion funding).

workers-first.evidence: Voted Yea on the Laken Riley Act, which requires DHS to detain certain unlawfully present people arrested for burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting; it passed the House 263-156 and became law Jan. 29, 2025.

prio.label: Matches 4 of 5 priorities; 1 backed by their record, 3 only promised

cands.bio: Republican U.S. representative from the Inland Empire, first elected in 1992 and in office since 1993. Chairs the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense. Former small business owner in restaurants and real estate. Chaired the Riverside County Republican Party from 1984 to 1988. Lives in Corona.

controversies.text: Federal records show $22,900 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; $269,239 from individuals passed through that PAC in 2025-26; 1 staff trip paid for by that foundation.
Missed 2 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (0.3%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 1, 2025-09-17 to 2025-09-17.

In December 2020 Calvert joined 125 other House members on a court brief backing Texas's suit over four states' election rules. The Supreme Court denied the suit on Dec. 11 for lack of standing. In January 2021 he voted to object to Arizona's and Pennsylvania's electoral votes. He said states' voting rules should be set by legislatures.

In November 1993, Corona police officers found Calvert in a parked car with a woman who was a convicted prostitute. He told them, "We're just talking." No arrest was made. After the Riverside Press-Enterprise went to court for the police report, Calvert publicly called his behavior "inappropriate."

endorsements.text: Steve Hilton (Republican nominee for governor) endorsed Calvert in 2026.
The California Republican Assembly and the California Congress of Republicans endorsed Calvert in 2026.
Donald Trump and the Republican Party of California endorsed Calvert in 2024.

cands.gaps: We found no documented statements or actions by Calvert on data centers, new development or growth limits, homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign land buyers, gun laws, or school choice and teacher pay. Nothing we read showed him taking a position on H-1B visas specifically. He did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey in 2020, 2022, 2024 or 2026. His campaign site is brief and does not list policy positions. The Wikipedia entry carries no readable source citations, so details such as the 1993 incident rest on that page alone.
